title: Weekly links October 2, 2026: insurance and entrepreneurship, recycling bribes into public services, labor slack in health, scaling cash, and more…
gist: David McKenzie's weekly development-economics link roundup highlights research showing that income insurance from a spouse's state job raised entrepreneurship in China, that bribes are sometimes recycled into public services in 'informal fiscal systems', that ChatGPT raises student output while causal-reasoning training improves depth of thinking, and that health-worker overload is not a generalized constraint in developing-country primary care.

insights.claim: In China after 1993, people whose spouse held a state job were 9.8 percentage points more likely to become entrepreneurs, more than double the pre-reform rate of 4.6%, with the effect scaling with the safety of the spouse's job.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Household income insurance, not just capital, unlocks entrepreneurship — relevant for designing social safety nets that foster startups.
insights.quote: people whose spouse held a state job were 9.8 percentage points more likely to become entrepreneurs, more than double the pre-reform rate of 4.6%

insights.claim: The entrepreneurship boost from a spouse's secure state job works as insurance: it is largest in families with volatile incomes, poor health or no health cover, and the resulting firms choose riskier industries and spend more on research.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Safety nets can shift new-firm creation toward higher-risk, R&D-intensive, growth-oriented ventures.
insights.locator: Johan Fourie on the way the

insights.claim: Research by Aman-Rana, Minaudier and Sukhtankar documents public employees paying for public services such as food banks, flood relief and police uniforms and vehicles themselves, partly funded by bribes extracted from citizens — what they call informal fiscal systems.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Official tax and spending figures understate the true fiscal footprint in resource-constrained states.
insights.locator: On VoxDev, Shan Aman-Rana, Clement Minaudier

insights.claim: Where governments are severely resource-constrained and corruption monitoring is hard, letting bureaucrats take bribes and redistribute part of them into services can be an attractive option that keeps official taxes low.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive governance equilibrium: anti-corruption drives may reduce service provision unless official revenue rises.
insights.quote: it can be easier to induce bureaucrats to redistribute the bribes they already take than to prevent them from taking bribes in the first place
insights.locator: On VoxDev, Shan Aman-Rana, Clement Minaudier

insights.claim: An experiment with Bocconi first-year undergraduates found ChatGPT raised performance — recommendations rated higher and closer to experts' solutions — while causal-reasoning training did not improve performance or add to GPT's effect.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Generative AI lifts measured output quality, supporting productivity-gain narratives in knowledge work.
insights.locator: On VoxEU, Chiara Fumagalli Alfonso Gambardella

insights.claim: Only students trained in first-principles causal thinking stated when their recommendations would fail, explained mechanisms, and produced ideas distinct from classmates, suggesting AI raises output quality but not depth or originality of thinking.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: AI may homogenize outputs; human causal reasoning remains a complementary differentiator.
insights.locator: On VoxEU, Chiara Fumagalli Alfonso Gambardella

insights.claim: Jishnu Das and colleagues find little evidence that heavy workloads are a generalized constraint on primary-care quality in developing countries: the average provider has substantial unused capacity, but the average patient visits a relatively busy provider.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Hiring more health workers alone may not raise care quality; the problem is distribution and effort, not headcount.
insights.quote: The average healthcare provider has substantial unused capacity, but the average patient visits a relatively busy provider.
insights.locator: Labor slack in the health sector

insights.claim: Healthcare providers in rural Senegal saw only 5–9 patients a day and spent under 2 hours total on consultations, yet interactions lasted just 3–6 minutes; in two Indian cities 45% of interactions had no other patients waiting, though 5% had more than 10 waiting.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Short consultations are not explained by workload — a quality and incentive problem.
insights.locator: Labor slack in the health sector

insights.claim: Give Directly, as it scales, is grappling with general-equilibrium effects, trade-offs between fraud and reach, and delivering cash-plus via cheap mentoring and coaching, and a project is having macroeconomists predict in advance the multiplier of cash transfers in Malawi from baseline data.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Ex-ante multiplier predictions will test how well macro models capture local cash-transfer spillovers.
